about.title: Does the series wander? (ADF)
about.summary_plain: Checks whether a series keeps returning to a stable level or wanders off, which decides whether it should be differenced before forecasting.
use_when: Before fitting a forecasting model that needs a stable series
Together with the KPSS test, which looks at the same question from the other side
avoid_when: The series is very short (under about 30 periods)
There is an obvious one-off break (use Zivot-Andrews)
data_needs: One numeric series over time (or a panel, tested per series)
assumptions: Regular time steps
Any trend is described by the chosen trend option
outputs: Statistic, p-value and a plain verdict
about.example: Weekly sales give p = 0.57: the series wanders, so difference it once.
about.expert_notes: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (statsmodels adfuller); H0: unit root. Lag length by AIC/BIC/t-stat; regression 'c', 'ct', 'ctt' or 'n'; MacKinnon p-values.

assumptions: The first periods are lost (one per difference)

data_needs: A numeric series over time and the season length
assumptions: The first season of data is lost
about.example: Week 53's sales minus week 1's sales a year earlier.

assumptions: All values are positive
outputs: The same columns on a log scale

about.title: Tuning inside a backtest
about.summary_plain: Runs a second, inner backtest inside each training window, so settings are tuned without peeking at the outer test periods.
use_when: You tune settings (orders, penalties) and want an honest final error
avoid_when: You do not tune anything
data_needs: A dataset with a time dimension and enough history for both levels
assumptions: Inner folds fit inside every outer training window
outputs: A plan whose folds carry inner folds
about.example: Outer: expanding window, 4 origins; inner: expanding window, 3 origins.

about.title: Find the AR and MA orders
about.summary_plain: Tries a grid of past-value (AR) and past-error (MA) orders for a forecasting model and picks the one with the best balance of fit and simplicity.
use_when: Before fitting an ARIMA or ARIMAX model
avoid_when: The series still wanders (difference first)
Very short series
data_needs: One stable numeric series over time (optional drivers)
assumptions: The best order is within the grid
outputs: The best orders, the full grid of scores
about.example: Out of p = 0..4 and q = 0..4, ARMA(2,1) has the lowest AIC.
about.expert_notes: Grid search of SARIMAX(p,d,q) fits by AIC/BIC/HQIC/AICc (statsmodels arma_order_select_ic style); failed fits are skipped and reported.

about.title: Find seasonal orders
about.summary_plain: Extends the order search to seasonal past values and errors, for series with a repeating pattern.
use_when: The series has a clear season that differencing alone does not remove
avoid_when: No seasonality (use the plain order search)
data_needs: One stable numeric series over time and the season length
assumptions: The best orders are within the grid
outputs: Best non-seasonal and seasonal orders, the grid of scores
about.example: SARIMA(1,0,1)(1,1,0)[52] wins on weekly sales.

vars.description: The series: variable names, or labels along the data's series dimension (every series of the target when omitted)

by_criterion.description: Lag by aic, bic, hqic, fpe

about.title: How many lags for series together
about.summary_plain: Picks how many past periods a model of several related series should use.
use_when: Before fitting a VAR or VECM
avoid_when: One series (use the AR/MA order search)
data_needs: Two or more stable numeric series over time
assumptions: The best lag is within the range
outputs: The selected lag by each criterion
about.example: AIC picks 3 lags, BIC 1.

vars.description: The series: variable names, or labels along the data's series dimension (every series of the target when omitted)

about.title: How many long-run ties
about.summary_plain: Decides how many long-run relationships tie a set of wandering series together, which the error-correction model needs.
use_when: Before fitting a VECM
avoid_when: The series do not wander
data_needs: Two or more wandering numeric series
assumptions: Johansen's assumptions (enough history, the right trend terms)
outputs: The selected rank and the test table
about.example: Rank 1 for three related prices.

about.title: Try settings on a backtest
about.summary_plain: Fits a model with each combination of settings you list, scores each on a backtest, and picks the best.
use_when: Tuning a few settings of any catalog model
avoid_when: Large grids on slow models (each point is a full fit per fold)
data_needs: A dataset, a split plan and the settings to try
assumptions: The backtest error reflects real use
outputs: The best settings and a table of scores
about.example: Try 3 saturation shapes x 2 carry-over lengths, keep the lowest MAPE.

split.description: A holdout plan (its split becomes data.split)

about.title: Fit a model
about.summary_plain: Fits any model from the catalog to the data, optionally scoring it on a test period, and saves it as a model version.
use_when: Every workflow that ends in a model
avoid_when: You only need data checks
data_needs: A dataset and the model's settings
assumptions: The model's own assumptions (see its About)
outputs: A model version with its scorecard and metrics
about.example: Fit ts.sarimax@^1 with order from the search node.

refit.description: Refit on every fold (else fit once and roll forward)

about.title: Backtest a model
about.summary_plain: Refits a model on every fold of a split plan and measures its forecast error at each horizon, so you see how reliable it really is.
use_when: Before trusting a forecasting model
Comparing models fairly
avoid_when: Slow models with many folds (each fold is a fit)
data_needs: A dataset, a split plan and the model settings
assumptions: Folds resemble how the model will be used
outputs: Metrics per fold and horizon, forecasts per fold
about.example: Ten folds of ARIMAX: MAPE 6% at 1 week, 11% at 8 weeks.

about.title: Forecast with a model
about.summary_plain: Uses a fitted model version to forecast ahead, with future drivers if it needs them.
use_when: Producing the forecast after a model was selected
avoid_when: The model cannot forecast (check its score modes)
data_needs: A model version and, for driver models, future driver values
assumptions: Future drivers are as planned
outputs: A forecast dataset and a fan chart
about.example: Forecast 12 weeks with planned prices.

season.description: Season length for MASE (default: from the frequency)

about.title: Measure forecast error
about.summary_plain: Measures how far a model's predictions were from what actually happened on the test data, in several easy-to-read ways.
use_when: After fitting or backtesting a model
avoid_when: Nothing was held out for testing
data_needs: A model version (and a test period) or backtest results
assumptions: The test data resembles future use
outputs: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE, range coverage, per horizon
about.example: MAPE 8% and 88% of actual values inside the 90% range.
about.expert_notes: MASE scales by the in-sample seasonal-naive MAE (Hyndman & Koehler 2006); CRPS from draws or quantiles.

about.title: Simple benchmark forecasts
about.summary_plain: Scores very simple forecasts, such as 'same as last week' or 'same as last year', on the same test periods, so you can check a model beats them.
use_when: Any forecasting workflow (a model must beat these to be worth it)
avoid_when: There is no time order
data_needs: A dataset and the same split plan the model used
assumptions: The benchmark is evaluated on exactly the same folds
outputs: Metrics of each benchmark per fold and horizon
about.example: Seasonal naive has MAPE 14%; the ARIMAX model 9%.

about.title: Check the model's errors
about.summary_plain: Checks the errors a model leaves behind for leftover patterns, uneven size and non-bell shapes, all in one go.
use_when: After fitting any time-series or regression model
avoid_when: Models without residuals (classifiers)
data_needs: A model version
assumptions: Residuals are available from the fit
outputs: Ljung-Box, normality and spread checks with plain verdicts, ACF of errors
about.example: No leftover pattern, slightly heavy tails, even spread.

about.title: Compare models side by side
about.summary_plain: Puts the scores of several models and benchmarks in one table so you can see which does best on each measure.
use_when: You fitted or backtested several candidates
avoid_when: Models were tested on different periods (the comparison would be unfair)
data_needs: Metrics from two or more model or benchmark nodes
assumptions: Everything was scored on the same folds
outputs: A comparison table and a ranking per metric
about.example: ARIMAX 9% MAPE, ETS 11%, seasonal naive 14%.

p_value.description: The p-value (median over series for panels)

reject.description: Whether the null hypothesis was rejected at alpha

decision.description: The decision label (see the test's About)

reject_share.description: Share of series where the null was rejected

about.title: Is one forecast really better?
about.summary_plain: Tests whether one model's forecasts are truly more accurate than another's or whether the difference could be luck.
use_when: Two models are close and you need to know if the gap is real
avoid_when: Very few test periods
data_needs: Backtest errors of two models on the same folds
assumptions: Error differences are stable over time
outputs: Statistic, p-value and which model is better
about.example: ARIMAX beats ETS but p = 0.31: the difference may be luck.
about.expert_notes: Diebold-Mariano test with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold small-sample correction on squared or absolute loss.

must_beat.description: Benchmark ids the winner must beat

selected_model.description: The winner's catalog model ref, when it is a model node

about.title: Pick the best model
about.summary_plain: Picks the model with the best score from a comparison, and can insist that it beats the simple benchmarks.
use_when: The end of a bake-off between candidates
avoid_when: Only one candidate
data_needs: A comparison table
assumptions: The chosen metric is the one that matters for the decision
outputs: The winning model version and why it won
about.example: Pick the lowest RMSE, but only if it beats seasonal naive by 5%.

about.title: Keep models that pass a bar
about.summary_plain: Keeps only the models whose score passes a limit you set, for example an error below 10%.
use_when: You need every model that is good enough, not just the best
avoid_when: You need exactly one winner
data_needs: A comparison table
assumptions: The limit reflects what is acceptable
about.example: Keep every model with MAPE under 10%.

policy.description: Policy id (default: the one in force)

submit.description: Submit the result for approval when the checks pass

about.title: Run the governance checks
about.summary_plain: Runs every check your organisation's policy requires on a model, such as beating random noise and a simple benchmark, and records the evidence.
use_when: Before a model may be validated and promoted
avoid_when: Exploratory work that will not be used
data_needs: A model version and the data it was fitted on
assumptions: The policy matches the model's family
outputs: Evidence for every check and an overall pass or fail
about.example: Seven checks pass, the placebo check fails: the model is not validated.

about.title: Run one governance check
about.summary_plain: Runs a single check from the governance catalog on a model, for example the shuffled result test.
use_when: Trying a check before adding it to a policy
avoid_when: Formal validation (run the whole policy)
data_needs: A model version and its data
assumptions: The check applies to the model's family
outputs: Evidence for the check and its pass, warn or fail
about.example: The noise-channel check gives the fake channel a 2% share: pass.

about.title: Plain-language report
about.summary_plain: Writes a short report of what the workflow found: test verdicts, the decisions taken, the chosen model and how well it does.
use_when: At the end of any workflow you share with others
avoid_when: You only need the raw numbers
data_needs: Results of earlier nodes
assumptions: Earlier nodes succeeded or were skipped for a reason
outputs: A report with text, tables and plots
about.example: Sales wander, so they were differenced; ARIMAX(2,1,1) beat seasonal naive by 30%.

about.title: Evidence pack
about.summary_plain: Bundles a model's governance evidence, decisions and approvals into one document for auditors, as HTML and JSON.
use_when: Audit, model risk review or sign-off
avoid_when: Before the governance checks have run
data_needs: A model version with governance evidence
assumptions: Evidence is stored for every check
about.example: A pack with 9 checks, 2 approvals and the lineage of model v7.

condition.description: Condition in the workflow expression language

about.title: Choose a path
about.summary_plain: Decides which way the workflow goes from earlier results, for example 'difference the series only if the tests say it wanders'.
use_when: A step should only run under a condition
avoid_when: Every step should always run
data_needs: Results of earlier nodes (and workflow parameters)
assumptions: The condition refers only to earlier nodes
outputs: The path taken (then or else) and the values that decided it
about.example: nodes.adf.p_value >= params.alpha or nodes.kpss.reject decides whether to difference.
about.expert_notes: Conditions use the safe expression language (mapi_spec.expr): comparisons, and/or/not, arithmetic, a few functions; no code is executed.

about.title: Run another workflow
about.summary_plain: Runs a saved workflow as one step of this one, so common sequences such as data readiness checks are written once and reused.
use_when: A sequence of steps is shared by several workflows
avoid_when: The steps are only used here
data_needs: A saved workflow revision and its inputs
assumptions: The other workflow's inputs and outputs match how it is wired here
about.example: Reuse 'time-series readiness' before three different model workflows.

about.title: Statistical test
about.summary_plain: Checks a property of the data or of a model's errors and gives a yes/no verdict with its evidence.
use_when: You need to decide something from the data (difference or not, which lags)
avoid_when: You only want a chart (use the Data Explorer)
data_needs: A dataset or a model version
assumptions: Each test's own assumptions (see its card)
outputs: Statistic, p-value, decision and a plain verdict
about.example: ADF says the series wanders.

about.title: Data processing
about.summary_plain: Changes the data before later steps use it, for example taking differences or logs.
use_when: Data must be prepared before a test or a model
avoid_when: The data is ready as it is
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: Transforms are undone on forecasts where needed
about.example: Difference sales once.

about.title: Decision
about.summary_plain: Chooses which path the workflow takes from earlier results.
use_when: A step should only run when a condition holds
avoid_when: Everything always runs
data_needs: Results of earlier nodes
assumptions: Conditions only read earlier results
about.example: Difference only when the series wanders.

about.title: Train/test plan
about.summary_plain: Decides which periods or groups the model learns from and which it is tested on, possibly many times over.
use_when: Every model you want to test honestly
avoid_when: You do not test the model
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: Test periods resemble how the model will be used
about.example: Six expanding-window folds.

about.title: Search
about.summary_plain: Tries many settings and picks the best by a score.
use_when: Choosing orders or settings from the data
avoid_when: Settings are fixed in advance
data_needs: A dataset (and a split plan for backtest searches)
assumptions: The best setting is in the search range
outputs: Best settings and a table of scores
about.example: Find ARMA orders by AIC.

about.title: Model
about.summary_plain: Fits, backtests or forecasts with any model from the catalog.
use_when: The workflow should produce a model or a forecast
avoid_when: Only data checks
data_needs: A dataset and model settings
assumptions: The model's own assumptions
about.example: Fit an ARIMAX model.

about.title: Evaluation
about.summary_plain: Measures how good a model or a simple benchmark is on test data.
use_when: After fitting or backtesting
avoid_when: Nothing was held out
data_needs: Model versions or backtests
assumptions: Test data resembles real use
about.example: Score the seasonal-naive benchmark.

about.title: Comparison
about.summary_plain: Puts several candidates' scores side by side, or tests whether one is truly better.
use_when: Several candidate models
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: Metrics of the candidates
assumptions: Same folds for every candidate
outputs: A comparison table or a test
about.example: ARIMAX vs ETS vs naive.

about.title: Selection
about.summary_plain: Picks the winner, or every candidate that passes a bar.
use_when: The end of a bake-off
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: A comparison table
assumptions: The metric reflects the decision
about.example: Lowest RMSE wins.

about.title: Governance
about.summary_plain: Runs the checks a model must pass before it can be validated, and stores the evidence.
use_when: Before validating or promoting a model
avoid_when: Throw-away experiments
data_needs: A model version and its data
assumptions: A policy covers the model's family
outputs: Evidence and a pass or fail
about.example: Run the tenant policy.

about.title: Report
about.summary_plain: Turns the workflow's results into a readable report or an evidence pack.
use_when: Sharing results
avoid_when: Nobody reads the result
data_needs: Earlier results
assumptions: Earlier nodes finished
about.example: A one-page summary.

about.title: Sub-workflow
about.summary_plain: Runs another saved workflow as one step.
use_when: Reusing a common sequence
avoid_when: One-off steps
data_needs: A saved workflow revision
assumptions: Inputs and outputs match
about.example: Reuse the readiness checks.

about.title: Time-series readiness to ARIMAX
about.summary_plain: Checks whether your series needs differencing, finds how many past values matter, backtests a forecast with drivers against simple benchmarks and only keeps it if it wins and passes governance.
use_when: You want an automatic, well-tested forecast of one series with drivers
You want every modelling decision recorded and explained
avoid_when: You have many related series that drive each other (use VAR/VECM)
You have fewer than about two seasons of history
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
Optional drivers known for the future (prices, holidays)
assumptions: Past patterns carry into the forecast horizon
Drivers affect the series linearly
outputs: Test verdicts and the differencing decision
Backtest errors by horizon vs benchmarks
about.example: Weekly orders: the tests say 'difference once', AIC picks (2,1,1), the backtest beats seasonal naive by 25% and governance passes.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice

season.description: Season length in periods (52 for weekly data)

horizons.description: Forecast horizons scored in the backtest

gap.description: Periods between training and test (late data)

drivers.description: Driver columns known for the future

data.description: The weekly (or daily) series to model

with.condition: (not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject)

about.title: Series that move together (VAR or VECM)
about.summary_plain: Tests whether several series are tied together in the long run and then models them together the right way, either keeping the long-run tie or working with their changes.
use_when: Two to five series influence each other (prices, sales, search interest)
avoid_when: A single series
Fewer than about 50 periods
data_needs: Two to five numeric series over time at the same frequency, one value per series and period (a long table, or a wide sheet ingested with the wide mapping)
assumptions: The relationships stay the same over the period
Effects work through past values
about.example: Your price and two competitors' prices share one long-run tie: a VECM with rank 1 shows gaps close within a month.

target.description: The main result (one of the series)

driver.description: A series that may help predict it

data.description: The series along one dimension (a value per series and period)

about.title: Marketing mix with governance
about.summary_plain: Checks your drivers, fits the marketing mix model, runs your organisation's governance checks and produces a report and an evidence pack for sign-off.
use_when: A marketing mix model will inform budget decisions
Model risk or audit needs evidence
avoid_when: Quick exploration (use the guided template)
data_needs: Weekly sales and spend per channel (by market if you have it)
assumptions: The governance policy for marketing mix models is set up
outputs: A report and an evidence pack
about.example: The model passes the shuffled-result and fake-channel checks and waits for a reviewer's approval.

drivers.description: Spend and control columns checked for collinearity

about.title: Forecast bake-off
about.summary_plain: Backtests several forecasting models on exactly the same periods, compares them with simple benchmarks and refits the winner.
use_when: You do not know which forecasting method suits your series
avoid_when: You already have a model you trust
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
assumptions: The backtest periods resemble the future
outputs: Backtest errors per model and horizon
about.example: ETS wins with 7% error at 4 weeks; ARIMA 8%, Theta 9%, seasonal naive 12%.

block.description: Periods shuffled together (default: about one season)

about.title: Beats a shuffled result
about.summary_plain: Refits the model on a copy of the data where the result column is shuffled at random; a real model must do clearly better on the true data than on noise.
use_when: Every model whose accuracy is used to make decisions
avoid_when: Models without a test period (there is nothing to compare)
data_needs: The model's data, its settings and a test period
assumptions: Shuffling breaks any real link between drivers and result
outputs: The share of shuffled fits that did as well as the real one (a p-value)
about.example: The real model's error is lower than all 20 shuffled fits: p = 0.0, pass.

references.title: Ojala & Garriga (2010), Permutation tests for studying classifier performance

about.expert_notes: Permutation (randomisation) test: the holdout metric of the real fit is compared with K refits on permuted targets (block permutation along time keeps the marginal distribution); p = (1 + #{perm <= real}) / (K + 1).

about.title: Ignores fake drivers
about.summary_plain: Adds a few made-up drivers that are pure noise and refits; a trustworthy model gives them almost no effect.
use_when: Marketing mix and other models that split a result between drivers
avoid_when: Pure forecasting models without drivers
data_needs: The model's data and settings
assumptions: The fake drivers look like real ones but carry no signal
outputs: The largest share of the result given to a fake driver
Whether any fake driver came out clearly non-zero
about.example: Three fake channels get 0.4%, 0.1% and 0.9% of sales: pass.
about.expert_notes: Placebo regressors drawn as Gaussian noise or as a driver shuffled in blocks; the statistic is the largest absolute contribution share (or the posterior probability that the effect exceeds a practical threshold).

checks.title: Effects vanish when shifted in time

about.title: Effects vanish when shifted in time
about.summary_plain: Moves the drivers months away from when they really happened and refits; the effects should mostly disappear, otherwise the model picks up timing patterns rather than real effects.
use_when: Models that credit results to drivers over time (marketing mix, regressions)
avoid_when: Very short series (the shift leaves too little overlap)
data_needs: The model's data and settings over time
assumptions: A real effect is tied to when the driver happened
outputs: Placebo effect as a share of the real effect, per shift
about.example: Shifting spend by half a year keeps only 8% of the effect: pass.
about.expert_notes: Time-shift placebo (leads/lags beyond any plausible carry-over); ratio of the placebo total effect to the real one, maximised over shifts.

about.title: Beats simple benchmarks
about.summary_plain: Compares the model's error on the test periods with very simple forecasts such as 'same as last week' or 'same as last year'; the model must be better.
use_when: Every forecasting model
avoid_when: Models that do not forecast over time
data_needs: The model's test periods and the history before them
assumptions: Benchmarks are scored on exactly the same periods
outputs: Skill against the strongest benchmark (1 - model error / benchmark error)
about.example: The model's error is 30% lower than 'same as last year': skill 0.30, pass.

references.title: Hyndman & Koehler (2006), Another look at measures of forecast accuracy

about.expert_notes: Relative skill 1 - L(model)/min_b L(b) on the holdout or backtest folds; MASE-style scaling by the in-sample seasonal-naive error is reported as well.

checks.title: No pattern left in the errors

about.title: No pattern left in the errors
about.summary_plain: Checks that the model's errors look like random noise over time; a leftover pattern means the model misses something it could have learned.
use_when: Time-series and regression models
avoid_when: Models without residuals
data_needs: The model's in-sample errors
assumptions: Regular time steps
outputs: The Ljung-Box p-value and the errors' autocorrelations
about.example: Ljung-Box p = 0.38 at 10 lags: pass.
about.expert_notes: Ljung-Box Q on residuals (model_df adjusted for ARMA terms); the minimum p-value over series for panels.

params.description: Parameters to watch (default: the key effects)

about.title: Estimates are stable over time
about.summary_plain: Refits the model on rolling windows of history and checks that its key estimates do not swing wildly from one window to the next.
use_when: Models whose estimates drive decisions (effects, returns)
avoid_when: Short histories (windows would be too small)
data_needs: The model's data over time and settings
assumptions: The true effects change slowly
outputs: How much each key estimate varies across windows
about.example: TV's return varies by 12% across windows: pass.
about.expert_notes: Coefficient of variation (or max relative deviation from the full-sample estimate) of each watched parameter across rolling-window refits; maximum over parameters.

about.title: Effects point the right way
about.summary_plain: Checks that effects have the direction business sense expects, for example that advertising does not reduce sales and that higher prices do not raise demand.
use_when: Any model with interpretable effects
avoid_when: Pure forecasting models
data_needs: The model's estimates and the expected directions
assumptions: The expected directions are right
outputs: The share of the estimate (or of the uncertainty) on the wrong side, per effect
about.example: Radio's effect is negative with 40% probability: fail.

about.title: Not driven by assumptions
about.summary_plain: Refits a Bayesian model with wider and narrower starting assumptions and checks the key answers barely move, so they come from the data.
use_when: Bayesian models, especially with business priors
avoid_when: Models that are not Bayesian
data_needs: The model's data, settings and priors
assumptions: Reasonable prior changes are covered by the scales tried
outputs: The largest relative change of a key estimate
about.example: Doubling prior widths moves TV's return by 6%: pass.

references.title: Kallioinen et al. (2023), Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling

about.expert_notes: Power-scaling or refit-based prior sensitivity: relative change of posterior means of key quantities under scaled prior widths.

about.title: Finds known answers
about.summary_plain: Simulates data from the model with known true values, refits, and checks that the model's ranges contain the true values about as often as they should.
use_when: New or heavily customised models
Before trusting a complex Bayesian model
avoid_when: Models that cannot simulate data
data_needs: The model's settings and data shape
assumptions: The simulated data resembles the real data
outputs: How often the 90% ranges contained the truth
about.example: True values fell inside the 90% ranges 88% of the time: pass.

references.title: Talts et al. (2018), Validating Bayesian inference algorithms with simulation-based calibration

about.expert_notes: Simulation-based calibration lite: N simulate-fit cycles; coverage of central 90% intervals and rank uniformity per parameter.

about.title: The fit finished properly
about.summary_plain: Checks that the fitting procedure settled on a stable answer, so running it again would give the same result.
use_when: Every model
avoid_when: Models fitted outside the platform without diagnostics
data_needs: The fit's diagnostics
assumptions: Diagnostics were recorded by the fit
outputs: R-hat, effective draws and divergences (Bayesian) or the optimiser status
about.example: All chains agree (R-hat 1.003): pass.
about.expert_notes: Bayesian: max split R-hat (rank-normalised), with ESS and divergences as evidence; frequentist: optimiser convergence flag (value 1.0 when converged, inf otherwise).

about.title: Accurate on unseen data
about.summary_plain: Checks the model's error on periods it was not fitted on stays below the limit your organisation sets.
use_when: Every model used for forecasts or what-ifs
avoid_when: Models without a test period
data_needs: A test period or backtest
assumptions: The test periods resemble future use
outputs: The chosen error metric on the test data
about.example: MAPE 9% against a limit of 15%: pass.

about.title: Data is good enough
about.summary_plain: Checks the data before trusting the model: few gaps, enough history, no constant columns and no impossible values.
use_when: Every model
avoid_when: Synthetic data you generated yourself
data_needs: The dataset the model was fitted on
assumptions: The limits fit your data
outputs: Data problems found, each in plain words
about.example: No gaps, 3 years of history, every driver varies: pass.

default_policies.name: Marketing mix models (platform default)
default_policies.description: Marketing mix models split results between channels, so they must beat shuffled results, give fake channels no credit and point effects the right way. Seeded for every tenant; edit it or add stricter project policies.

default_policies.name: Forecasting models (platform default)
default_policies.description: Forecasts must beat simple benchmarks out of sample, stay accurate on unseen periods and leave no pattern in their errors. Seeded for every tenant.

default_policies.name: Regression and machine-learning models (platform default)
default_policies.description: Tabular and choice models must beat shuffled results and stay accurate on unseen data; fake drivers should get no credit. Seeded for every tenant.

about.title: Beats simple benchmarks
about.summary_plain: Compares the model's error on the test periods with very simple forecasts such as 'same as last week' or 'same as last year'; the model must be better.
use_when: Every forecasting model
avoid_when: Models that do not forecast over time
data_needs: The model's test periods and the history before them
assumptions: Benchmarks are scored on exactly the same periods
outputs: Skill against the strongest benchmark (1 - model error / benchmark error)
about.example: The model's error is 30% lower than 'same as last year': skill 0.30, pass.

references.title: Hyndman & Koehler (2006), Another look at measures of forecast accuracy

about.expert_notes: Relative skill 1 - L(model)/min_b L(b) on the holdout or backtest folds; MASE-style scaling by the in-sample seasonal-naive error is reported as well.

about.title: The fit finished properly
about.summary_plain: Checks that the fitting procedure settled on a stable answer, so running it again would give the same result.
use_when: Every model
avoid_when: Models fitted outside the platform without diagnostics
data_needs: The fit's diagnostics
assumptions: Diagnostics were recorded by the fit
outputs: R-hat, effective draws and divergences (Bayesian) or the optimiser status
about.example: All chains agree (R-hat 1.003): pass.
about.expert_notes: Bayesian: max split R-hat (rank-normalised), with ESS and divergences as evidence; frequentist: optimiser convergence flag (value 1.0 when converged, inf otherwise).

about.title: Data is good enough
about.summary_plain: Checks the data before trusting the model: few gaps, enough history, no constant columns and no impossible values.
use_when: Every model
avoid_when: Synthetic data you generated yourself
data_needs: The dataset the model was fitted on
assumptions: The limits fit your data
outputs: Data problems found, each in plain words
about.example: No gaps, 3 years of history, every driver varies: pass.

about.title: Accurate on unseen data
about.summary_plain: Checks the model's error on periods it was not fitted on stays below the limit your organisation sets.
use_when: Every model used for forecasts or what-ifs
avoid_when: Models without a test period
data_needs: A test period or backtest
assumptions: The test periods resemble future use
outputs: The chosen error metric on the test data
about.example: MAPE 9% against a limit of 15%: pass.

about.title: Ignores fake drivers
about.summary_plain: Adds a few made-up drivers that are pure noise and refits; a trustworthy model gives them almost no effect.
use_when: Marketing mix and other models that split a result between drivers
avoid_when: Pure forecasting models without drivers
data_needs: The model's data and settings
assumptions: The fake drivers look like real ones but carry no signal
outputs: The largest share of the result given to a fake driver
Whether any fake driver came out clearly non-zero
about.example: Three fake channels get 0.4%, 0.1% and 0.9% of sales: pass.
about.expert_notes: Placebo regressors drawn as Gaussian noise or as a driver shuffled in blocks; the statistic is the largest absolute contribution share (or the posterior probability that the effect exceeds a practical threshold).

about.title: Beats a shuffled result
about.summary_plain: Refits the model on a copy of the data where the result column is shuffled at random; a real model must do clearly better on the true data than on noise.
use_when: Every model whose accuracy is used to make decisions
avoid_when: Models without a test period (there is nothing to compare)
data_needs: The model's data, its settings and a test period
assumptions: Shuffling breaks any real link between drivers and result
outputs: The share of shuffled fits that did as well as the real one (a p-value)
about.example: The real model's error is lower than all 20 shuffled fits: p = 0.0, pass.

references.title: Ojala & Garriga (2010), Permutation tests for studying classifier performance

about.expert_notes: Permutation (randomisation) test: the holdout metric of the real fit is compared with K refits on permuted targets (block permutation along time keeps the marginal distribution); p = (1 + #{perm <= real}) / (K + 1).

about.title: Effects vanish when shifted in time
about.summary_plain: Moves the drivers months away from when they really happened and refits; the effects should mostly disappear, otherwise the model picks up timing patterns rather than real effects.
use_when: Models that credit results to drivers over time (marketing mix, regressions)
avoid_when: Very short series (the shift leaves too little overlap)
data_needs: The model's data and settings over time
assumptions: A real effect is tied to when the driver happened
outputs: Placebo effect as a share of the real effect, per shift
about.example: Shifting spend by half a year keeps only 8% of the effect: pass.
about.expert_notes: Time-shift placebo (leads/lags beyond any plausible carry-over); ratio of the placebo total effect to the real one, maximised over shifts.

about.title: Effects point the right way
about.summary_plain: Checks that effects have the direction business sense expects, for example that advertising does not reduce sales and that higher prices do not raise demand.
use_when: Any model with interpretable effects
avoid_when: Pure forecasting models
data_needs: The model's estimates and the expected directions
assumptions: The expected directions are right
outputs: The share of the estimate (or of the uncertainty) on the wrong side, per effect
about.example: Radio's effect is negative with 40% probability: fail.

about.title: Finds known answers
about.summary_plain: Simulates data from the model with known true values, refits, and checks that the model's ranges contain the true values about as often as they should.
use_when: New or heavily customised models
Before trusting a complex Bayesian model
avoid_when: Models that cannot simulate data
data_needs: The model's settings and data shape
assumptions: The simulated data resembles the real data
outputs: How often the 90% ranges contained the truth
about.example: True values fell inside the 90% ranges 88% of the time: pass.

references.title: Talts et al. (2018), Validating Bayesian inference algorithms with simulation-based calibration

about.expert_notes: Simulation-based calibration lite: N simulate-fit cycles; coverage of central 90% intervals and rank uniformity per parameter.

about.title: No pattern left in the errors
about.summary_plain: Checks that the model's errors look like random noise over time; a leftover pattern means the model misses something it could have learned.
use_when: Time-series and regression models
avoid_when: Models without residuals
data_needs: The model's in-sample errors
assumptions: Regular time steps
outputs: The Ljung-Box p-value and the errors' autocorrelations
about.example: Ljung-Box p = 0.38 at 10 lags: pass.
about.expert_notes: Ljung-Box Q on residuals (model_df adjusted for ARMA terms); the minimum p-value over series for panels.

about.title: Not driven by assumptions
about.summary_plain: Refits a Bayesian model with wider and narrower starting assumptions and checks the key answers barely move, so they come from the data.
use_when: Bayesian models, especially with business priors
avoid_when: Models that are not Bayesian
data_needs: The model's data, settings and priors
assumptions: Reasonable prior changes are covered by the scales tried
outputs: The largest relative change of a key estimate
about.example: Doubling prior widths moves TV's return by 6%: pass.

references.title: Kallioinen et al. (2023), Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling

about.expert_notes: Power-scaling or refit-based prior sensitivity: relative change of posterior means of key quantities under scaled prior widths.

about.title: Estimates are stable over time
about.summary_plain: Refits the model on rolling windows of history and checks that its key estimates do not swing wildly from one window to the next.
use_when: Models whose estimates drive decisions (effects, returns)
avoid_when: Short histories (windows would be too small)
data_needs: The model's data over time and settings
assumptions: The true effects change slowly
outputs: How much each key estimate varies across windows
about.example: TV's return varies by 12% across windows: pass.
about.expert_notes: Coefficient of variation (or max relative deviation from the full-sample estimate) of each watched parameter across rolling-window refits; maximum over parameters.

about.title: Customer choice
about.summary_plain: Explains which product a customer picks on each shopping trip and how price and promotions change that choice.
use_when: You have purchase records with the price of every product on offer
You want to test a price change before making it
avoid_when: You only have total sales, not individual choices
data_needs: One row per trip: the product chosen and each product's price and promotion
assumptions: Customers pick the option they like best given price and promotion
Taste differences between households are stable over time
outputs: How sensitive choices are to price and promotion
about.example: A 10% cut in Brand A's price moves its share from 30% to 36%.

references.title: McFadden (1974), Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior

about.expert_notes: Conditional (McFadden) logit over alternative-specific covariates with household random effects; Bayesian-bootstrap draws over households.

about.title: Marketing mix model
about.summary_plain: Measures how much each marketing channel adds to your sales, in total or per market, and shows what would happen if you moved budget between channels.
use_when: You have two or more years of weekly sales and spend per channel
You want to know the return of each channel and plan budgets
You have results per market or product and want them modelled together
avoid_when: Spend barely changes over time (the effect cannot be measured)
You have less than a year of history
You need answers in seconds (use the fast frequentist version)
data_needs: Weekly (or daily) sales, spend per channel, and optional controls such as price
assumptions: Advertising has a lingering effect and diminishing returns
Things that drive both spend and sales are included as controls
outputs: Contribution and return per channel with ranges
about.example: TV returns 2.1 euros per euro spent (range 1.4 to 2.9) and search 3.4.

references.title: Jin et al. (2017), Bayesian methods for media mix modeling with carryover and shape effects

about.expert_notes: mmm-framework BayesianMMM: geometric/Weibull adstock, Hill or logistic saturation, trend options, Fourier seasonality, hierarchical pooling over geos and products (MFF panels); priors from business beliefs; lift tests as calibration likelihood; NUTS via PyMC, nutpie or numpyro.

about.title: Fast marketing mix model
about.summary_plain: Gives a quick first estimate of each channel's contribution in seconds, without the ranges a full Bayesian model provides.
use_when: You need a fast first look before a full model
You want to compare many set-ups quickly
avoid_when: Decisions depend on how certain the answer is
You want to bring in business beliefs or lift tests
data_needs: Weekly sales and spend per channel
assumptions: Carry-over and saturation settings are searched over a grid
Channel effects are not negative
outputs: Contribution and return per channel (bootstrap ranges optional)
about.example: A first read in 5 seconds: TV 28% of sales, search 12%.
about.expert_notes: mmm-framework frequentist ridge / constrained least squares with a grid search over transform parameters; optional bootstrap.

about.title: Predict a number with ranges you can add up
about.summary_plain: Fits the same method many times on resampled data, which gives ranges that stay correct when you add predictions up into totals.
use_when: You need a range for totals (all stores, a whole region)
The data has groups (stores) that should be resampled together
avoid_when: You need results in seconds on a very large table (it fits many models)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: Rows you predict look like the rows the model learnt from
Resampling whole groups captures how uncertain the model is
outputs: Many joint simulated predictions per row
about.example: A range for next month's total sales across 300 stores.
about.expert_notes: A bootstrap ensemble (optionally resampling whole groups with 'by'); each replicate is a joint draw, so aggregation is valid (draws representation).

about.title: Predict yes or no
about.summary_plain: Estimates the chance that something happens for each row of a table, such as a customer buying again or an order arriving late.
use_when: The result is yes or no for each row
You want a probability to rank or target rows
avoid_when: The result is a number or has more than two outcomes
data_needs: A table with a yes/no column and the columns that explain it
assumptions: Rows you score look like the rows the model learnt from
outputs: The probability of 'yes' for each row
about.example: The chance each customer orders again next month, to decide who gets a voucher.
about.expert_notes: An allow-listed scikit-learn or xgboost binary classifier on stacked rows; point representation of the positive-class probability.

about.title: Predict a number with a guaranteed range
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each row with a range that contains the true value about as often as you ask for, such as nine times out of ten.
use_when: You need ranges whose coverage you can rely on, row by row
You do not want to make assumptions about the shape of the errors
avoid_when: You need ranges for totals (use the bootstrap version)
You have very little data (part of it is kept aside to size the ranges)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: New rows behave like the rows kept aside for sizing the ranges
outputs: One prediction and a range per row
about.example: Ranges that hold next week's demand for 90% of store-product pairs.
about.expert_notes: Split-conformal prediction intervals at level 1 - alpha with a calibration fraction; marginal per-cell coverage; interval representation (not aggregatable).

about.title: Predict a number with a low and high estimate
about.summary_plain: Predicts a low, middle and high value for each row of a table, so you see how sure the prediction is.
use_when: You need a best and worst case per store, product or customer
Stock or staffing decisions depend on the high or low end
avoid_when: You need to add predictions up into totals with a range (ranges per row cannot be added)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: Rows you predict look like the rows the model learnt from
outputs: A low, middle and high prediction per row
about.example: Plan stock at the 90% level: the high estimate of next week's demand per store.
about.expert_notes: xgboost multi-quantile regression or one scikit-learn quantile model per level; quantile representation (per-cell quantiles cannot be aggregated across cells).

about.title: Predict a number from a table
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each row of a table, such as a store and week, from the other columns, using a well-known machine-learning method you pick.
use_when: You have many rows with drivers (price, promotion, weather) and want one best guess per row
You want to see how much each driver adds to a prediction
avoid_when: You need a range of likely values (use the quantile, bootstrap or conformal versions)
You have a single short series over time
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: Rows you predict look like the rows the model learnt from
Future values of the drivers are known when you forecast
outputs: Each driver's contribution (linear and tree models)
about.example: Predict next week's units per store and product from planned prices with gradient boosting.
about.expert_notes: An allow-listed scikit-learn or xgboost regressor on rows stacked from the labelled dims (coordinates become features); point representation; exact linear or counterfactual-zeroing contributions; models stored as skops or xgboost JSON.

about.title: Group effects with sharing
about.summary_plain: Estimates a separate baseline for every group, such as a county or a store, while letting small groups borrow strength from the others.
use_when: Groups have very different amounts of data
You want to predict for groups you have not seen yet
avoid_when: You have a single series over time
data_needs: One row per observation with a group label and predictors
assumptions: Groups are alike enough that sharing information is sensible
Effects are additive on the model's scale
about.example: Radon levels per house, with each county's baseline pulled towards the state average when the county has few houses.
about.expert_notes: Bayesian hierarchical GLM (PyMC, NUTS): partially pooled group intercepts and optional slopes; group-level covariates in the mean; new levels drawn from the fitted hyperprior.

about.title: Demand by store and week
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each store, product and week from prices, promotions and the calendar, with a low and a high estimate.
use_when: You have many stores or products and want a forecast for each
Prices, promotions or stock explain demand
avoid_when: You need to add predictions up into totals with a range (ranges cannot be added)
You have a single short series
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and its drivers, per store and week
assumptions: Future values of the drivers are known when you forecast
Stores the model has not seen behave like the average store
outputs: A median forecast with low and high values per cell
about.example: Predict next week's units for 300 stores from planned prices and promotions.
about.expert_notes: Gradient-boosted quantile regression (xgboost or sklearn) on stacked rows; coordinates become categorical features; direct multi-horizon forecasting; quantile representation (no cross-cell aggregation).

about.title: Effects that build up over time
about.summary_plain: Explains a series from its own past and the current and past values of drivers, so you can see how an effect builds up over several periods.
use_when: A driver's effect is spread over several periods
avoid_when: Effects are immediate only (a simple regression is enough)
data_needs: One result and one or more drivers over time
assumptions: Drivers affect the result, not the other way round
The series vary around stable levels or share a long-run relationship
about.example: A promotion lifts sales 8% in its week and 3% the week after.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ARDL with lag orders chosen by information criterion (ardl_select_order).

about.title: Forecast from past values
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series from its own recent past and trend, without outside drivers.
use_when: You have only the series itself
You want a solid, well-known forecasting method
avoid_when: Outside drivers explain most of the movement (use the version with drivers)
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: After differencing, the series varies around a stable level
about.example: Forecast monthly sales 6 months ahead from the last few years of sales.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s (state space) without exog.

about.title: Common movements across many series
about.summary_plain: Finds a few hidden forces that move many series together, such as the overall economy behind sales in many categories.
use_when: You have many related series and want their shared drivers
avoid_when: You have one or two series
data_needs: Many numbers over time at the same frequency
assumptions: A few common factors explain most of the joint movement
outputs: How strongly each series follows them
about.example: Twenty category sales series follow one 'consumer mood' factor.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels DynamicFactor (state space; factors follow a VAR).

about.title: Long-run and short-run effects
about.summary_plain: Separates the short-term effect of a driver from its long-term effect on one series, and tests whether a long-run relationship exists at all.
use_when: One result and a few drivers trend together
You want both the immediate and the lasting effect of a driver
avoid_when: Neither the result nor the drivers trend (a regression with lags is enough)
data_needs: One result and one or more drivers over time
assumptions: Drivers affect the result, not the other way round
about.example: A 1% price rise cuts sales 0.4% at once and 1.1% in the long run.

references.title: Pesaran, Shin & Smith (2001), Bounds testing approaches

about.expert_notes: Single-equation error-correction model in UECM form (statsmodels UECM); Pesaran-Shin-Smith bounds test for a levels relationship.

about.title: Exponential smoothing forecast
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series by giving recent values more weight than older ones, with optional trend and seasonality, and is quick and robust.
use_when: You need a fast, reliable baseline forecast
The level, trend and seasonality shift slowly
avoid_when: Outside drivers explain most of the movement
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: Recent history is the best guide to the near future
about.example: Forecast monthly demand 12 months ahead with a damped trend.

references.title: Hyndman et al., Forecasting with Exponential Smoothing

about.expert_notes: statsmodels ETSModel (error, trend, seasonal; additive or multiplicative; damped trend) with simulation-based prediction intervals.

about.title: Hidden states over time
about.summary_plain: Finds a small number of hidden states, such as calm and busy periods, that a series switches between, and says which state each period was probably in.
use_when: Your series seems to switch between distinct modes
avoid_when: Behaviour changes smoothly rather than in jumps
You have very short sequences
data_needs: One or more sequences of measurements over time
assumptions: Each state has its own typical level and spread
The chance of switching depends only on the current state
outputs: The likely state of each period
about.example: An animal's track splits into resting and travelling phases.
about.expert_notes: K-state Gaussian HMM; states marginalised with the forward algorithm in PyMC; terminal state stored for forecast and filter; label switching fixed by ordering.

about.title: Smooth trend forecast
about.summary_plain: Forecasts one regular series with a smooth, flexible trend and a repeating seasonal pattern, and gives a range of likely values.
use_when: You forecast one weekly or daily series with a trend that bends over time
You want an honest range around the forecast
avoid_when: You have many related series (forecast them together or per store)
You need to forecast further ahead than the model allows without refitting
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: The trend changes gradually
The seasonal pattern repeats
about.example: Forecast weekly website visits 26 weeks ahead with a 90% range.

references.title: Riutort-Mayol et al. (2022), Practical Hilbert space approximate Bayesian Gaussian processes

about.expert_notes: Hilbert-space Gaussian process (HSGP) trend with optional linear drift and Fourier seasonality (PyMC, NUTS); forecasts limited to max_extension periods.

about.title: Switching between regimes
about.summary_plain: Detects whether a series switches between regimes, such as high-growth and low-growth periods, and estimates the behaviour in each.
use_when: Behaviour seems to jump between distinct modes
You want the probability of being in each mode now
avoid_when: Changes are gradual
You have little history
data_needs: One number over time, plus optional drivers
assumptions: A small number of regimes; switching depends only on the current regime
outputs: Probability of each regime per period
about.example: Demand switches between a normal and a promotion-driven regime.

references.title: Hamilton (1989), A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series

about.expert_notes: statsmodels MarkovRegression / MarkovAutoregression (Hamilton filter, EM then BFGS).

about.title: Forecast with past values and drivers
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series from its own recent past, its seasonal pattern and outside drivers you know ahead, such as planned prices or holidays.
use_when: You forecast one regular series a few periods ahead
Known future drivers (prices, promotions, holidays) matter
avoid_when: You have less than about 50 periods
Several series drive each other (use VAR)
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency, plus optional driver columns known for the future
assumptions: After differencing, the series varies around a stable level
Relationships stay the same over time
about.example: Forecast weekly orders 12 weeks ahead from orders in recent weeks and planned discounts.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (ch. 9-10)

about.expert_notes: statsmodels SARIMAX (state space): ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s with exogenous regressors; exact likelihood via the Kalman filter; prediction intervals as quantiles; future exog required for forecasts.

about.title: Simple strong baseline
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series by combining a straight-line trend with smoothed recent values, a simple method that is hard to beat.
use_when: You want a strong, simple baseline to compare other models against
avoid_when: Outside drivers matter a lot
You need detailed explanations
data_needs: One number over time (seasonality is removed and put back automatically)
assumptions: The recent trend continues
about.example: A theta forecast of monthly sales to beat before using anything more complex.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ThetaModel (Assimakopoulos-Nikolopoulos; equivalent to SES with drift) with optional seasonal decomposition.

about.title: Trend, season and noise
about.summary_plain: Splits a series into a slowly changing level and trend, a seasonal pattern and noise, and forecasts it from those parts.
use_when: You want to see the underlying trend without the noise
The trend and season change slowly over time
avoid_when: You only need a quick baseline (exponential smoothing is simpler)
data_needs: One number over time, plus optional drivers
assumptions: Each part changes smoothly and independently
about.example: Weekly sales split into a rising trend, a Christmas peak and week-to-week noise.

references.title: Harvey, Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter

about.expert_notes: statsmodels UnobservedComponents (local level/trend, stochastic seasonal, cycle, exog) estimated by maximum likelihood with the Kalman smoother.

about.title: Series that drive each other
about.summary_plain: Models several series that influence each other over time, such as prices and sales of two brands, and forecasts them together.
use_when: Several series move together and affect each other
You want to see how a shock to one series spreads to the others
avoid_when: You have one series
Series trend together for good (use the error-correction model)
data_needs: Two or more numbers over time at the same frequency
assumptions: Each series varies around a stable level, after differencing if needed
Effects work through past values
outputs: Which series help predict which (Granger tests)
about.example: A price cut by brand A lowers brand B's sales for three weeks.

references.title: Lutkepohl, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis

about.expert_notes: statsmodels VAR(p): OLS per equation; lag order by AIC/BIC/HQIC; impulse responses and forecast-error variance decomposition; Granger causality tests.

about.title: Series that drive each other, with drivers
about.summary_plain: Models several series that influence each other and also respond to outside drivers you know ahead, and forecasts them together.
use_when: Several series affect each other and outside drivers matter too
avoid_when: You have one series
You have many series and little history
data_needs: Two or more numbers over time, plus driver columns known for the future
assumptions: Series vary around stable levels
Driver effects are steady
about.example: Forecast sales of two brands from each other's history and planned promotions.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels VARMAX(p,q) with exogenous regressors (VARX when q = 0); estimated by maximum likelihood in state-space form.

about.title: Series tied together for good
about.summary_plain: Models series that wander but stay tied together in the long run, such as prices of close substitutes, and shows how fast they snap back after a gap opens.
use_when: Series trend but keep a stable long-run relationship
avoid_when: Series do not trend
The long-run tie is not plausible
data_needs: Two or more trending numbers over time
assumptions: A stable long-run relationship exists (checked by the Johansen test)
about.example: When a competitor's price drifts 5% above yours, half the gap closes within 4 weeks.

references.title: Johansen (1991), Estimation and hypothesis testing of cointegration vectors

about.expert_notes: statsmodels VECM with cointegration rank from the Johansen trace/max-eigenvalue tests; deterministic terms selectable.

about.title: Decision
about.summary_plain: Chooses which path the workflow takes from earlier results.
use_when: A step should only run when a condition holds
avoid_when: Everything always runs
data_needs: Results of earlier nodes
assumptions: Conditions only read earlier results
about.example: Difference only when the series wanders.

about.title: Comparison
about.summary_plain: Puts several candidates' scores side by side, or tests whether one is truly better.
use_when: Several candidate models
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: Metrics of the candidates
assumptions: Same folds for every candidate
outputs: A comparison table or a test
about.example: ARIMAX vs ETS vs naive.

about.title: Evaluation
about.summary_plain: Measures how good a model or a simple benchmark is on test data.
use_when: After fitting or backtesting
avoid_when: Nothing was held out
data_needs: Model versions or backtests
assumptions: Test data resembles real use
about.example: Score the seasonal-naive benchmark.

about.title: Governance
about.summary_plain: Runs the checks a model must pass before it can be validated, and stores the evidence.
use_when: Before validating or promoting a model
avoid_when: Throw-away experiments
data_needs: A model version and its data
assumptions: A policy covers the model's family
outputs: Evidence and a pass or fail
about.example: Run the tenant policy.

about.title: Model
about.summary_plain: Fits, backtests or forecasts with any model from the catalog.
use_when: The workflow should produce a model or a forecast
avoid_when: Only data checks
data_needs: A dataset and model settings
assumptions: The model's own assumptions
about.example: Fit an ARIMAX model.

about.title: Report
about.summary_plain: Turns the workflow's results into a readable report or an evidence pack.
use_when: Sharing results
avoid_when: Nobody reads the result
data_needs: Earlier results
assumptions: Earlier nodes finished
about.example: A one-page summary.

about.title: Search
about.summary_plain: Tries many settings and picks the best by a score.
use_when: Choosing orders or settings from the data
avoid_when: Settings are fixed in advance
data_needs: A dataset (and a split plan for backtest searches)
assumptions: The best setting is in the search range
outputs: Best settings and a table of scores
about.example: Find ARMA orders by AIC.

about.title: Selection
about.summary_plain: Picks the winner, or every candidate that passes a bar.
use_when: The end of a bake-off
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: A comparison table
assumptions: The metric reflects the decision
about.example: Lowest RMSE wins.

about.title: Train/test plan
about.summary_plain: Decides which periods or groups the model learns from and which it is tested on, possibly many times over.
use_when: Every model you want to test honestly
avoid_when: You do not test the model
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: Test periods resemble how the model will be used
about.example: Six expanding-window folds.

about.title: Sub-workflow
about.summary_plain: Runs another saved workflow as one step.
use_when: Reusing a common sequence
avoid_when: One-off steps
data_needs: A saved workflow revision
assumptions: Inputs and outputs match
about.example: Reuse the readiness checks.

about.title: Statistical test
about.summary_plain: Checks a property of the data or of a model's errors and gives a yes/no verdict with its evidence.
use_when: You need to decide something from the data (difference or not, which lags)
avoid_when: You only want a chart (use the Data Explorer)
data_needs: A dataset or a model version
assumptions: Each test's own assumptions (see its card)
outputs: Statistic, p-value, decision and a plain verdict
about.example: ADF says the series wanders.

about.title: Data processing
about.summary_plain: Changes the data before later steps use it, for example taking differences or logs.
use_when: Data must be prepared before a test or a model
avoid_when: The data is ready as it is
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: Transforms are undone on forecasts where needed
about.example: Difference sales once.

about.title: Forecast bake-off
about.summary_plain: Backtests several forecasting models on exactly the same periods, compares them with simple benchmarks and refits the winner.
use_when: You do not know which forecasting method suits your series
avoid_when: You already have a model you trust
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
assumptions: The backtest periods resemble the future
outputs: Backtest errors per model and horizon
about.example: ETS wins with 7% error at 4 weeks; ARIMA 8%, Theta 9%, seasonal naive 12%.

about.title: Marketing mix with governance
about.summary_plain: Checks your drivers, fits the marketing mix model, runs your organisation's governance checks and produces a report and an evidence pack for sign-off.
use_when: A marketing mix model will inform budget decisions
Model risk or audit needs evidence
avoid_when: Quick exploration (use the guided template)
data_needs: Weekly sales and spend per channel (by market if you have it)
assumptions: The governance policy for marketing mix models is set up
outputs: A report and an evidence pack
about.example: The model passes the shuffled-result and fake-channel checks and waits for a reviewer's approval.

about.title: Time-series readiness to ARIMAX
about.summary_plain: Checks whether your series needs differencing, finds how many past values matter, backtests a forecast with drivers against simple benchmarks and only keeps it if it wins and passes governance.
use_when: You want an automatic, well-tested forecast of one series with drivers
You want every modelling decision recorded and explained
avoid_when: You have many related series that drive each other (use VAR/VECM)
You have fewer than about two seasons of history
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
Optional drivers known for the future (prices, holidays)
assumptions: Past patterns carry into the forecast horizon
Drivers affect the series linearly
outputs: Test verdicts and the differencing decision
Backtest errors by horizon vs benchmarks
about.example: Weekly orders: the tests say 'difference once', AIC picks (2,1,1), the backtest beats seasonal naive by 25% and governance passes.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice

about.title: Series that move together (VAR or VECM)
about.summary_plain: Tests whether several series are tied together in the long run and then models them together the right way, either keeping the long-run tie or working with their changes.
use_when: Two to five series influence each other (prices, sales, search interest)
avoid_when: A single series
Fewer than about 50 periods
data_needs: Two to five numeric series over time at the same frequency, one value per series and period (a long table, or a wide sheet ingested with the wide mapping)
assumptions: The relationships stay the same over the period
Effects work through past values
about.example: Your price and two competitors' prices share one long-run tie: a VECM with rank 1 shows gaps close within a month.
